Our Debian Jessie review said it slices a few seconds off boot times but is removable with little fuss for those who would prefer to go their own way at startup time.

But it's still there; it has to be, because some services are installing without init scripts these days, relying entirely on systemd, and systemd itself has usurped the function of many core services. That's why cooking up a Debian fork that is fully functional without so much as a shred of systemd is actually impressive: they've removed its tendrils in a much more thorough way than simply changing your init daemon.

The really sad part is that systemd -- the real, central core of systemd: the init daemon -- is beautiful for its intended purpose; that is, speeding up the boot process by turning what has traditionally been a single-threaded init into a multi-threaded init. For a desktop environment, that may only equate to a few seconds shaved off of an occasional boot, but in a cloud, where thousands of ephemeral servers are created and destroyed every hour, it can come out to real, quantifiable savings/earnings. If they had stuck with that and perfected it rather than branching out and consuming half the fucking processes in the base install of any distro, there would be no controversy, and Unix admins everywhere, greybeards and ladyfaces alike, would be rejoicing.
